our-team.html: Meet the people behind Mahurangi West Pest. Together, our team provides leadership and support for restoration projects, pest control initiatives, fundraising, communications, and community engagement across Mahurangi West.

volunteer-with-us.title: Volunteer With Us
volunteer-with-us.html:
Make a Difference in Mahurangi West

Our volunteers are at the heart of everything we do. Together, we’re restoring native habitats, protecting wildlife, and creating a healthier environment for future generations. Whether you have a few hours a month or more time to give, every contribution makes a real difference. No previous experience is needed – just a willingness to help and learn.

Why Volunteer?

Volunteering with Mahurangi West Pest is a rewarding way to give back to your community while helping protect the unique environment we all enjoy.

As a volunteer, you’ll:

  • Help protect native birds, wildlife, and forests.
  • Contribute to the restoration of the Mahurangi West peninsula.
  • Gain practical conservation and environmental experience.
  • Learn new skills through training and hands-on volunteering.
  • Meet like-minded people who are passionate about conservation.
  • Enjoy spending time outdoors in beautiful surroundings.
  • Build valuable experience to include on your CV or job applications.
  • Demonstrate your commitment to your community and the environment.
  • Be eligible for volunteer references (where appropriate).
  • Make a lasting difference for local wildlife and future generations.

Volunteer Roles

There are many ways you can get involved, depending on your interests, skills, and availability.

  • Trapping – Monitor and maintain pest traps and record catches in Trap.NZ
  • Hub Coordinator – Support volunteers within a local hub by coordinating trap servicing, welcoming new volunteers, and acting as a point of contact.
  • Planting/Weeding – Help with native planting and weed control days
  • Community Events – Assist with community events, displays, working bees, fundraising, or educational activities.
  • Administration & Communications – Help behind the scenes with a variety of administrative, organisational, and communication tasks that support our projects and volunteers.
  • Monitoring & Citizen Science – Assist with bird counts, coastal wildlife monitoring, and other conservation projects.

Current Volunteer Vacancies

  • Hub Coordinator 5
  • Hub Coordinator 8

Join Our Volunteer Team

Whether you’re interested in trapping, planting, administration, or helping at events, we’d love to welcome you. Even if you don’t see a role that matches your interests, please get in touch. We’d love to find a way for you to be involved.

Join now

Together, we can create a healthier, pest-free Mahurangi West for generations to come.

about-us.title: About Us
about-us.html:
Mahurangi West Pest began in 2019 covering an area of about 2,100 ha and now controls some 3,500 ha. Our pest control group comprises approx. 200 properties and over 150 volunteers in the areas known as Mahurangi West and Hungry Creek and was formed to develop and implement a plan for pest control in line with Pest Free Auckland 2050.

Our volunteers bring together a diverse array of backgrounds and experience to – control plant and animal pests through the development of a long-term sustainable control programme, to help re-establish healthy native bush and thriving native wildlife.

An Auckland Council grant pays for a part-time community coordinator.

donate.title: Donate
donate.html:
Mahurangi West Pest is a community-led initiative working to protect and restore our local bush, wetlands, and native wildlife through ongoing predator control.

Every donation directly helps us to maintain trap lines, monitor wildlife, support volunteers, and employ local paid trappers to expand our work across Mahurangi West. Predators such as rats, stoats, and possums have a major impact on native wildlife, and sustained trapping helps create safer habitats and healthier ecosystems.

mahurangi-west-pest.title: Mahurangi West Pest Inc.
mahurangi-west-pest.html:
Who we are

150+ Volunteers on the Mahurangi West peninsula targeting animal pests and invasive weeds, carrying out bird and bat monitoring, and generally working to enhance biodiversity and the health of our wonderful environment.

Featured

Micro-volunteering

You want to get involved and give back to the community, but can’t fit another big commitment into your busy schedule? Then micro-volunteering might just be the thing.

Micro-volunteering is a small, bite-sized task or project, that is quick and easy to perform. For example, it only takes 30 minutes to do a bird count, and just four times a year (to cover the four seasons). You could check a trap line (including resetting and baiting) in about half an hour. Checking community traps (where there are generally just 3-5) can be done in 15-20 minutes.

Volunteer Opportunities

We rely on over 150 volunteers to achieve our goals of a pest free environment. Why not join us? There will also be opportunities to do some plantings and/or weed control in the future. If you find yourself with free time on your hands on the weekend, or during the week, we’d love to hear from you. Not only will you help a good cause, but it can also be a way to meet people and learn new skills.

Another way of helping is through donations, which are 100 percent used to provide pest control tools and resources for volunteer field events.

blog.title: Mahurangi West Pest Blog
blog.html:
First Kereru fledgling seen in 19 years

“Thank you fellow trappers”, says Mike Jenkin. “If anyone doubted the value of your volunteer work see the video on Mahurangi West Pest’s Facebook page which I took of a mum feeding its baby. This is the first Kereru fledgling I have seen from my deck in 19 years in the Bay.”

Grant to Find, Research and Protect our Native Bat

Mahurangi West Pest was recently successful in obtaining a $5,000 grant from Auckland Council Environmental Services for research into the long-tailed bat or pekapeka-tou-roa.

Bird of the Year

A few feathers were ruffled last year when the pekapeka-tou-roa was voted New Zealand’s Bird of the Year!  Peter Wills, Campaign Manager for the bat entry, says it was a matter of supporting the ‘underbird’, which has a status of ‘nationally threatened’ in conservation and received a bad rap from the Covid-19 pandemic.

Nationally, the awareness of the bats had been lifted, and Mahu West Pest saw an opportunity for bats which may call our community ‘home’.

Funding to help our local efforts  

Nada Cottrell, Mahurangi West Pest Funding Coordinator, says the team decided to apply for the funding grant and was successful in receiving $5,000 towards work to find and protect bats on the Mahurangi West peninsula.

She says their first objective, with the support of volunteers and the use of acoustic listening devices, is to be able to identify any bats that might be in the area.

“If found, we’ll then work to provide awareness for the community and training for volunteers in best practice to support our local bats.”

Long-term, Nada says, Mahurangi West Pest would like to help establish and maintain a viable long-tailed bat population on the peninsula.

Local volunteers and landowners

Mahurangi West Pest are now looking for local volunteers who would like to learn more about assisting with bat research in Mahurangi West, such as learning about acoustic listening devices for bats, and/or supporting bat habitats.

We also would like to hear from land-owners who are willing for on-the-ground research to take place on their land.

If you are interested, please contact: nada.mahuwestpest@gmail.com

How to help the bat

Information from Auckland Environmental Services suggest land owners can do the following to support our native bats:

  • Retain standing dead trees and old-age trees with cavities. Bats breed in cavities in old-aged trees, moving to a new roost tree regularly, returning later to reuse it. Social groups may use over 100 different roosting trees. If felling a woodlot, check trees for cavities first. 
  • Protect cabbage trees and other lone native trees on farmland as important roosts. Replant natives to shelter and ensure their long term survival.  
  • Protect old-age willow and mature natives around ponds where bats feed, e.g. aquatic insects over water. Overhanging trees around ponds help bats feed in poor weather.
  • Reduce the use of pesticides negatively impacting bats.

Bat Fact

“A Long-tailed Bat (pekapeka-tou-roa) weighs about the same as New Zealand’s $2 coin.”

plant-pests.title: Pest Plants
plant-pests.html:
And Control Methods

  • Buffer Zone Programme
  • Cape Ivy
  • Climbing Asparagus
  • Bushy Asparagus
  • Cotoneaster
  • Monkey Apple Tree
  • Moth Plant
  • Pampas Grass
  • Tradescantia (Wandering Willie)
  • South American Pampas Grass
  • Wild Ginger
  • Woolly Nightshade

Buffer Zone Programme –
Pest Plant Control starts November 2022

A park buffer zone is a 500m area surrounding a park with special ecological values. In park buffer zones there are restrictions on selected highly invasive pest plants to prevent them spreading into the parks. These pest plants degrade native habitats by smothering native plants and killing them, removing habitat and food sources for our native animals. By controlling these pests we are helping the native habitats to flourish, supporting healthy ecosystems and a wide range of Auckland’s wonderful wildlife.

Properties around Mahurangi Regional Park are in a buffer zone. Auckland Council is controlling pest plants on the park, and these now need to be controlled on the buffer zone land as well.

Free control of climbing asparagus (shown above) and bushy asparagus in the buffer zone began earlier this year. There was great support from the community with that first round of control and we’re looking forward to another successful round.

Council will be in touch with eligible residents/owners of properties around Mahurangi Regional Park – please keep an eye out for this correspondence.

For information on the pest plants that are part of this work, and for more information on the programme, please visit www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/buffers

The buffer programme is part of Auckland Council’s Regional Pest Management Plan (RPMP). There are rules about management of some pest plants on properties in buffer zones.

When these pest plants are being managed on the park:

Climbing asparagus (shown above) and bushy asparagus – Auckland Council must undertake initial destruction on land in the buffers. Follow up destruction must be undertaken by the land owner/occupier.

Woolly nightshade, moth plant, and wild ginger – Land owners/occupiers of a buffer must undertake destruction of these plants on their land.

Which plant smells like turpentine when its leaves are crushed?

If you guessed woolly nightshade you’re doing well. Its stems are covered in small silica hairs that cause skin irritation too – best to cover up when getting rid of it from your property.

Woolly Nightshade (Solanum mauritianum)

A soft leaved perennial herb that can grow up to 3m tall. Small woolly nightshade plants are single stemmed, but become multi-stemmed as they mature.

If you occupy land within the buffer area of a park where woolly nightshade is being managed, you must destroy all woolly nightshade on that land.

Control Recommendations

For small stems cut near ground and paste with double strength glyphosate or picloram gel or frill stem and paste fresh cuts with double strength glyphosate gel or picloram gel. Note: Avoid using picloram near streams and wetlands.

Trees are best controlled standing and allowed to breakdown slowly. Follow up treated areas 3 times per year.

Woolly nightshade plants can cause irritation to the throat and skin. Wear a mask and long-sleeved shirt.

Physical control

Dig or pull out. Trunks and stems are slightly woody but easily chopped down with a hand saw.

Seeds require disposal – remove to greenwaste or landfill if practicable.

Cape Ivy (Senecio angulatus)

This plant pest belongs to the daisy family. Cape ivy is a scrambling perennial from Africa, that spreads through its fluffy, wind-blown seed. It can form dense mats, smothering plants to 3 metres tall and preventing native seedlings from growing.

It likes waste places, roadsides and the edges of coastal or regenerating lowland forests. It is most easily controlled during flowering and before seed is produced. It’s yellow flowers form in clusters, not unlike ragwort.

Hand pull small plants or dig out roots (all year round), then dispose of at a refuse transfer station, burn or bury deeply.

To eradicate Cape ivy

Stump swab (all year round): glyphosate (100ml/L) or metsulfuron-methyl 600g/kg (1g/L).

Cut stems below waist height, spray below this point (spring-summer to actively growing plants): glyphosate (10ml/L (knapsack) or 2L/100L (spraygun)) or metsulfuron-methyl 600g/kg (2g/10L (knapsack) or 20g/100L (spraygun)) or a product containing 100g picloram+300g triclopyr/L (60ml/10L) or a product containing 200g 2,4-D+100g dicamba/L (12ml/L) or dicamba 50g/L (24ml/L) or amitrole (150ml/15L (knapsack) or 2L/100L (spraygun)). Add penetrant to all mixes. [Weedbusters]

What can be done to stop it coming back?

Cut out or poison stumps. Remove dropped stems and dispose of as they can resprout. Reseed or replant bare areas.

Climbing Asparagus (Asparagus scandens)

A climbing vine from South Africa with feathery leaves and long wiry stems. The roots are fleshy tubers, which can survive for a long time and will re-sprout easily. Tiny white flowers appear in spring, which are followed by orange-red berries.

The berries can be dispersed over a wide area by birds to form new areas of invasion, and new growth will sprout readily from the tubers. The vine grows in a wide range of conditions including moderate to deep shade, moderate to heavy rainfall, and a wide range of temperatures and soil types, meaning it can invade and grow in most locations.

Climbing asparagus can form dense areas of growth on the ground, and will rapidly grow up plants, smothering the understorey up to a height of 4 metres. The vine can even ringbark trees and shrubs that have soft bark, killing them.

The dense areas of growth on the ground prevents native seedlings from establishing. Larger trees can be smothered and killed. This canopy loss lets more sunlight into the forest understory, which promotes the further invasion of weeds. As the vine climbs up the native trees it takes over areas where epiphytes would normally grow, further reducing diversity of native plants. This destruction of native plants can also contribute to erosion.

To eradicate climbing asparagus:

a) Cut growth approx. 50 cm from the ground and leave the upper part of the vine in the tree to die; ensure it is not touching the ground as it could re-sprout. Dig out the tuber and dispose of it to landfill.
or
b) Pull the vine well away from desirable plants and spray with glyphosate (20ml per litre of water) –ensure the spray is directed away from the desirable plant.

Follow up treatments will be required every 3-4 months, so check the treated area for regrowth regularly and respray or dig out tubers that have re-sprouted.

After 2-4 treatments, densely plant the area to minimise risk of re-invasion. Use native plants such as Muehlenbeckia complexa (Pohuehue) or Hen and Chicken fern. Continue to check area for any regrowth.

Bushy Asparagus (Asparagus aethiopicus)

A scrambling, multi-stemmed, bushy herb, also known as Asparagus densiflorus and its origin is South Africa. The roots are tuberous and form a thick mat. Flowers are white and borne in October – March.

If you occupy land within the buffer zone of a park where bushy asparagus is being managed, and Auckland Council has carried out initial destruction of bushy asparagus on that land, you must undertake follow up the destruction of all bushy asparagus on that land.

Habitats

Forest, scrub, coastal ecosystems, dunes.

Dispersal

Seeds dispersed by birds.

Impact on Environment

Can form dense infestations, excluding native vegetation. May impede recreational access to natural areas.

Control

Cut and pull vines away from desirable trees and native plants before foliar spraying. Follow up treated areas 3 times per year. Encourage natural regeneration of native plants or replant treated areas where possible after 2-3 treatments to establish dense ground cover and minimise re-invasion.

Physical control

Method: dig out.

Plant parts requiring disposal: Tubers, rhizomes and seeds.

Disposal options: Rot tubers, rhizomes and seeds in covered water barrel or remove to greenwaste or landfill if practical.

Community agrichemical control recommendations

With no qualifications: Foliar spray with 200ml glyphosate green per 10L of water.

Certified Handler/Experienced agrichemical user: Foliar spray with 200ml glyphosate green per 10L of water and 10ml penetrant.

Monkey Apple Tree
(Syzygium smithii or Acmena smithii)

The Monkey Apple is a rapidly growing, long-lived tree, originating from Australia. It has glossy oval leaves and can grow up to 15 metres tall. White to cream flowers appear during October to January, followed by bunches of small white to pinkish/mauve berries.

The berries are favoured by birds which then disperse the seed over wide areas.

Monkey Apple seedlings are shade tolerant and grow more rapidly than native seedlings. They will out-compete natives in the understorey and can form dense stands, altering the forest structure and replacing natives in the canopy.

Monkey Apple trees are hard to kill. Small seedlings can be dug out and left to rot. For large trees fell the tree and paint the fresh stump with Metsulfuron gel. Any fruit present should be removed and sent to landfill as they will germinate freely if left on the ground.

Inspect the treated area regularly (e.g. 6-monthly) to check for any sprouting seedlings. Replant densely with natives such as Titoki (Alectryon excelsus) to inhibit any new growth.

Cotoneaster (Cotoneaster glaucophyllus,
C. franchetii and C. simonsii)

Cotoneaster are small-leaved evergreen shrubs growing up to 4m tall. Small white/pink flowers appear in early summer, and these are followed by orange-red berries which can last on the tree up until mid-winter. Cotoneaster grows in a range of habitats including open scrubland, coastal forest, along road margins and coastal cliff tops. The shrubs grow rapidly to form dense stands, crowding out native plants and stopping native seedlings establishing. Birds love the berries and will contribute to dispersing the seeds over wide areas.

To control Cotoneaster fell the tree and paint the stump with metsulfuron gel 1-2mm thick. Care must be taken when using metsulfuron around non-target plants as they can also be poisoned. Glyphosate is less toxic and can be used as an alternative. If berries are present when felling the tree try to remove these if possible, and dispose to landfill, as they can germinate readily. Check the treated areas several times over the next year for any regrowth or new seedlings.

Replant the treated area after 6-12 months to establish thick ground cover to prevent re-infestation. Suggested native plants to use include Korokia, Karamū and Coastal mahoe.

Moth Plant (Araujia sericifera syn. A. hortorum)

This perennial climbing vine has milky sap/latex. Its stems are twining, scrambling and woody. Leaves have dull green tops and grey undersides. Fruit is fleshy, leathery and pear-shaped.

If you occupy land within the buffer area of a park where moth plant is being managed, you must destroy all moth plant on that land.

Habitats

Forest, forest margins, tracks, coastline, cliffs, shrublands, mangroves, wasteland, orchards, urban areas.

Dispersal

Seeds dispersed by wind and water.

Impact on environment

Smothers native vegetation and prevents recruitment. Potential to catastrophically impact forest structure. Poisonous milky latex in stems, leaves and roots can cause dermatitis.

CONTROL

Site Management

Cut and pull vines away from desirable trees and native plants before foliar spraying. Follow up treated areas 3 times per year. Encourage natural regeneration of native plants or replant treated areas where possible after 2-3 treatments to establish dense ground cover and minimise reinvasion.

PHYSICAL CONTROL

Method: Dig or pull out.

Plant parts requiring disposal: Seed pods.

Disposal options: Remove to greenwaste or landfill.

Biocontrol

Moth plant beetle (Colaspis argentinensis). For more information about how biocontrol works, see What is biocontrol?

Community agrichemical control recommendations

With no qualifications: Cut stump and paste freshly cut base of stems with metsulfuron gel.

Basic Growsafe certified: Cut stump and spray freshly cut base of stems with 1g metsulfuron-methyl per 1 L of water.

Certified Handler/Experienced agrichemical user: Foliar spray with 5g metsulfuron-methyl per 10L of water and 20ml penetrant.

Control requires tracing back all stems to the base stem, cutting it off and applying chemical to the base. All pods should be collected and destroyed safely prior to seeds being released.

Tradescantia fluminensis (Tradescantia fluminensis)

Plant Pest: Tradescantia fluminensis

Photo: Carolyn Lewis.

Source: http://www.weedbusters.org.nz

Tradescantia fluminensis, otherwise known as Wandering Willie, is a creeping dark green ground cover that grows happily in light to deep shade. It will form dense mats, smothering native plants and preventing growth of native seedlings. Small white flowers are present in December to January.

The plant is shallow rooted so can easily be pulled out or raked up however it can regrow from any small piece of stem that is left behind. Parts removed can be disposed of to landfill, burnt, or placed in a weed composting bag for 12 months. Or spray the plant with Triclopyr (6ml / Litre of water) with added penetrant. Care must be taken not to spray non-target plants as these can also be killed by this herbicide. Check the area regularly for regrowth as several applications at 2 – 3 month intervals may be required to successfully eradicate the weed. The Auckland Council website also lists some forms of biological control that are available for this weed.

Once eradicated, replant the area with dense ground cover plants (e.g. Nertera depressa or Adiantum aethiopica) to prevent reinvasion.

Plant Pest: Tradescantia fluminensis

Photo: Trevor James

Source: http://www.weedbusters.org.nz

………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………..

South American Pampas Grass
(Cortaderia sellonia and C. jubata)

Plant Pest: South American Pampas Grass

Source: pestsearch.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz

South American pampas grass is a large clump forming grass which can grow up to 4 metres tall. It grows rapidly, quickly colonising cleared land to form a dense ground cover that suppresses native plants and stops their regeneration. Pampas grass can become a fire hazard and provides a habitat for rats and other vermin. The plant spreads easily with seeds being blown long distances by winds. Seeds can also be dispersed by water, contaminated machinery or by animals.

South American pampas grass can appear similar to native toetoe, so it is important to differentiate the two before removing the plant. Pampas flowers late January to June with dense, erect flower heads. Toetoe flowers September to January and has drooping flower heads. The dead leaves of pampas forms spirals like wood shavings around the base of the plant, while toetoe does not form these spirals. The leaf base of toetoe is white and waxy whereas the leaf base of pampas is not waxy.

To control pampas:

If small enough, dig out the entire plant including roots and dispose of seed heads and roots to landfill.

Or        Fell the plant and paint the cut area with glyphosate gel.

Or        Spray entire plant with glyphosate foliage spray.

Check the treated area regularly for regrowth or reinfestation.

Once eradicated replant the area with plants such as native toetoe or Chionochloa species. This will help shade out pampas grass and stop it regrowing.

For photos and further information click on link below:

https://pestsearch.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/pest-search/Corjub

Wild Ginger (Hedychium gardnerianum
and H. flavescens)

Also known as Kahili ginger, this is a perennial herb that grows up to 3m tall. Flowers are fragrant and large rhizomes grow underground and above the ground. A perennial herb up to 3m tall. Surface rhizomes are large and branching. Leaves are large and green. Flowers are scented, borne in spikes, yellow with red stamens in H. gardnerianum and creamy yellow in H. flavescens. Fruits are fleshy and orange.

If you occupy land within the buffer area of a park where wild ginger is being managed, you must destroy all wild ginger on that land

Habitats

Forest, forest and riparian margins, shrublands, fernland.

Dispersal

H. gardnerianum seed dispersed by birds. Vegetative spread from rhizome fragments. Human-mediated dispersal through dumping of garden waste.

Impact on environment

Forms dense stands, suppressing native vegetation and preventing recruitment. Potential to change forest composition. May increase erosion and alter decomposition and nutrient cycling patterns.

CONTROL

Site Management

Follow up treated areas 3 times per year. Encourage natural regeneration of native plants or replant treated areas where possible after 2-3 treatments to establish dense ground cover and minimise reinvasion.

Recommended approaches

PHYSICAL CONTROL

Method: Cut stems and dig out rhizomes.

Plant parts requiring disposal: Seeds and rhizomes.

Disposal options: Small amounts can be rotted in a covered water barrel or remove to greenwaste or landfill.

Biocontrol: is currently not available for this species.

Community agrichemical control recommendations

With no qualifications:

For small infestations only: Cut stump and paste freshly cut rhizomes with a small amount of metsulfuron gel.

Basic Growsafe certified: Cut stump and spray freshly cut base with 1g metsulfuron-methyl per 1 L of water. For areas of wild ginger under native forest reduce rates to 0.5g metsulfuron-methyl per 1 L of water.

Caution: When using any herbicide or pesticide please read the label thoroughly to ensure that all instructions and safety requirements are followed.

A fast growing plant that forms large clumps. As wild ginger grows, more and more rhizomes are grown and these can stack up on each other out of the soil.

Very good at producing seed, wild ginger can quickly spread through native bush. Stems and leaves are soft and can easily be cut away.

Wild ginger can grow in low light conditions, expanding through native forests with ease. As the clumps are so dense, native seeds are unable to germinate on the ground.

Care must be taken when controlling ginger to remove all rhizomes as new plants can grow from fragments.

Wild ginger can survive in full sun conditions and the heat and dry. It is found in native forests, roadsides, pine forests, and anywhere that plants have been dumped.

Wild ginger flowers are born on long stems and are yellow with long necks. Orange anthers grow on long stems from the centre of each flower.

Commonly found in areas with other weed species where soil has been disturbed and native vegetation has been removed. Wild ginger can be controlled with herbicide that must be able to penetrate into each rhizome.

achieving-a-pest-free-peninsula.title: A Pest-Free Peninsula
achieving-a-pest-free-peninsula.html:
Setting trap lines

View our video on setting a humane Timms possum trap.

Facebook Link

Why we need to eliminate three major pest groups (mustelids, possums and rats) throughout New Zealand . . . See below:

Mustelids

Stoats, ferrets, and weasels are predators of native birds, eggs, lizards and insects. Weasels in particular, will tackle a prey much larger than themselves and nesting birds are easy targets. Control programmes to manage these pests, are essential for the survival of New Zealand’s special native species and ecosystems.

Possums

Possums threaten New Zealand’s ecology because they can increase to population densities where their browsing pressure can defoliate canopy and understorey vegetation. They also compete with and prey on our native fauna. Possums are an introduced species to New Zealand, brought here from Tasmania and Australia in the 1800s. The native species of NZ didn’t evolve with possums and thus don’t have natural defense mechanisms to protect them from this pest.

Rats

Non-native rodents, which originally hitched a ride to New Zealand on ships centuries ago, have proliferated to such an extent that they are now partially responsible for the endangerment of many of New Zealand’s native species. Ship rats, Norway rats and native kiore have a major impact in New Zealand because they are omnivores – eating birds, seeds, snails, lizards, fruit, weta, eggs, chicks, larvae and flowers.

Control, Monitor, Adapt, Enhance and Repeat to Protect Mahurangi West

Brian Bramell, Chair MWP

iwi.title: Iwi
iwi.html:
There are several iwi whānau with longstanding connections to the Mahurangi West Pest project area. These whānau continue to play an important role in the protection, restoration, and stewardship of the whenua.

Ngāti Maraeariki ki Mahurangi has longstanding ancestral ties to the area, including the ancestral pā sites of Maki, Korotangi. Members of Ngāti Maraeariki ki Mahurangi have been actively involved in both the planning and implementation of the Mahurangi West Pest project since its early stages, working alongside the wider community to help establish some of the first traplines across these lands. Whānau members Mel Whaanga, iwi advisor to the Mahurangi West Pest executive committee, and his daughter Anasazi Whaanga Green, a member of the committee, continue to play an active role in supporting the organisation’s ongoing restoration and conservation work throughout Mahurangi West area.

The Morehu Whānau owns land on Jamieson Bay Road. In partnership with the community, a grant application was made in 2021 to the Rodney Healthy Harbours programme to support pine tree removal, restoration, and native replanting on this Māori land.

The Roberts Whānau owns land in Opahi Bay, where members of the community established one of the early traplines as part of the pest control programme.

Mahurangi West Pest values the guidance, participation, and partnership of iwi and local whānau in caring for and restoring the natural environment of Mahurangi West.

Mel Whaanga has also shared the Ngāti Maraeariki ki Mahurangi Community Facebook page, which contains historical photographs and information relating to Ngāti Maraeariki ki Mahurangi settlement in Opahi Bay and Sullivans Bay (formerly known as Otarawao).

https://www.facebook.com/Ngati-Maraeariki-1812037695767852/

trap-lines-and-target-areas.title: Information Hub
trap-lines-and-target-areas.html:
Our aim is to eradicate pest animals from the Mahurangi West peninsula. The three main pest species we’re targeting are possums, mustelids (ferrets, stoats, weasels) and rodents (rats, mice) – in line with the Pest Free Auckland guidelines.

Target areas or hubs

We’ve developed nine trapping hubs (with support from the Auckland Council’s Biodiversity Team) to enable a coordinated approach in our trapping efforts. Each hub has a team of volunteers and landowners – overseen by a Mahurangi West Pest ‘area or hub coordinator’.

9 Hubs_Rds_Hubs_Named.png

Our trapline volunteers

Our trapline volunteers are the incredible people who give their time to check the traps and bait stations. They’re trained and supported by their area coordinator, on how to check, reset or rebait the traplines regularly. They also receive regular communication through our monthly newsletter or our Facebook group.

Traps

We use and maintain humane traps within – Timms possum traps, Victor rat traps and DOC200 for stoats, ferrets and weasels.

Tracking our progress

To track our progress, we use Trap.NZ to log the location of the traplines, record the type of pest killed, as well as the type of bait used in the traps and bait stations.

By using Trap.NZ across all of our hubs or target areas, we can collectively record all the data for Mahurangi West Pest to gain a picture of our work and share it with others.    

Collective data

A key benefit of using Trap.NZ is our data is automatically combined with thousands of other community pest projects around NZ. This helps to build a larger picture of how Aotearoa is progressing towards a Pest Free NZ 2050.

Your help with trapping

If you’re interested in volunteering your time to check a local trapline, we’d love to hear from you.

Or if you currently have your own traps on your property around Mahurangi West, and would like to join our project on Trap.NZ to add your progress along with the group, please get in touch.

our-volunteer-bird-counters.title: Bird Counts
our-volunteer-bird-counters.html:
We are training a dedicated bird counting group and, in time, rallying support for targeted bush regeneration and tree planting events.

Why Count Birds?

Any landcare group carrying out pest control needs to assess the birdlife at the beginning of their trapping as a benchmark and to carry out regular monitoring to see if their trapping efforts overtime are having the desired effect on the area’s bird populations.

In December 2020, some of our fledgling bird counters drove north to the Baddeleys Beach/Campbells Bay area to meet with Ngaire Wallen who coordinates the bird counters for the Takatu Landcare Group, which does volunteer conservation and restoration work on land near or adjacent to the Tawharanui Regional Park. For more information on the Takatu Landcare Group visit their website at: https://www.naturespace.org.nz/groups/takatu-landcare-group

Ngaire kindly agreed to show our group the ropes and took us to two places where she does a quarterly bird count – the first was a few hundred metres upstream with a view of mature forest on a ridge and the second on the beach at the mouth of its estuary. Her counters record the species and number of birds (and whether they are seen or just heard) for half an hour at each spot they monitor. The counts cover the four seasons and are routinely carried out at the same time and date each year.

Our fledgling volunteer bird counters get expert tutelage from Ngaire Wallen, who coordinates the bird counters for the Takatu Landcare Group.

eBirders and Reporting

Like Ngaire, we will update a spreadsheet quarterly with our group’s findings and then post the data on eBird – an online worldwide database run by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. This data also populates the New Zealand Bird Atlas.

For more information on eBird and eBirders see: https://ebird.org/newzealand/about

Recording seasonal data on Trap.NZ

From Autumn 2022 we have recorded each season’s bird counts onto Trap.NZ’s website. We currently have around 20 bird monitoring stations, where some 20 volunteers collect and submit data on birds (domestic and native) as part of our ongoing Mahurangi West Bird Project. For more about Trap.NZ visit: https://trap.nz/

A Trap.NZ screenshot showing our 20 bird monitoring stations across Mahurangi West.
